Your editor asks you to cover a demonstration by parents who are protesting cuts in the local school system—and to shoot some video with your phone, complete with B-roll and on-screen text. What should you edit it with? “There’s something on your computer,” she replies. “I forget the name of it. You went to Northeastern. I’m sure you can figure it out.” Or imagine you are working in the communications department of a social-service agency. Your manager wants you to put together a map plotting the location of all 12 of the agency’s branch officers, with photos, descriptions and links to more information. Where would you begin? Those are just two of the skills we will practice in Digital Storytelling and Social Media, a course in which we will use a variety of tools to tell stories with visuals, data and social networks. We will emphasize digital tools that are free or inexpensive. You will learn not just how to make a video that’s better than what you see on many newspaper websites and how to use Twitter to report a story; you will also learn how to be resourceful so that you can adapt to new tools on the fly. Over the course of the semester you will practice blogging, social-media journalism, mapping and smartphone photography and video. You will also learn a little bit about data visualization as well as how to use a content-management system (CMS) and how to do a little bit of coding in HTML. We will also explore how internet-based technologies are changing journalism and redefining how journalists do their jobs. Citizen media pioneer Dan Gillmor has called our readers (and viewers and listeners) the “former audience,” meaning that technology has empowered them not to be passive consumers of news and information, but to take part in the conversation. Journalists must be prepared to take part in that conversation as well. This course will consist of some lecturing, a lot of web and multimedia demonstrations, extensive classroom discussions, readings, in-class workshops and guest speakers. By the end of the semester, you will be familiar with the concepts and trends that are revolutionizing the way we think about journalism. This is a time of great pessimism about traditional forms of journalism such as newspapers, magazines and television. I hope you will all become forward-looking optimists over the next few months.
